title: Der arme Müllerbursch und das Kätzchen
titleEn: The Poor Miller's Boy and the Little Cat
part: The Poor Miller's Boy and the Little Cat
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 106. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, Thür, that, thun, gethan). The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 106 follows Hans, the miller's youngest and least-regarded apprentice, whom the other two abandon in a cave on the road. There he serves an enchanted little cat and her household of cats for seven years — sweeping, chopping wood, and, in the end, building her a tiny house with a silver axe — before she rewards his patience with the finest horse and the mill itself. A quiet, patient tale about being underestimated.

sentences.t: In einer Mühle lebte ein alter Müller, der hatte weder Frau noch Kinder, und drei Müllerburschen dienten bei ihm.
sentences.l: In a mill lived an old miller, he had neither wife nor children, and three miller’s-lads served with him.
sentences.i: In a mill there lived an old miller who had neither wife nor children, and three miller’s lads were in his service.
sentences.n: der hatte is a demonstrative picking up ein Müller, not a relative pronoun — German runs on where English subordinates. weder … noch is “neither … nor”. bei jemandem dienen is to be in someone’s service. Paragraph breaks are an addition here: the 1857 edition sets the whole tale as one block, which is hard going on a screen. The words between the breaks are the book’s.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun etliche Jahre bei ihm gewesen waren, sagte er eines Tags zu ihnen „ich bin alt, und will mich hinter den Ofen setzen:
sentences.l: When they had now been with him some years, he said one day to them “I am old, and will set myself behind the stove:
sentences.i: When they had been with him some years, he said to them one day, “I am old, and mean to sit myself down behind the stove;
sentences.n: wie here is “when”. etliche is an older “several, a good few”. eines Tags is a genitive of time, “one day”, where modern German writes eines Tages. The bench behind the great tiled stove is the warm corner of the house where the old sit, so sich hinter den Ofen setzen is to retire.

sentences.t: zieht aus, und wer mir das beste Pferd nach Haus bringt, dem will ich die Mühle geben, und er soll mich dafür bis an meinen Tod verpflegen.“
sentences.l: set out, and whoever brings me the best horse home, to that one I will give the mill, and he shall for that keep me until my death.”
sentences.i: set out, and whoever brings me home the best horse, to him I will give the mill, and he shall keep me for it until my death.”
sentences.n: zieht aus is the imperative of separable ausziehen, to set out; the shared glossary answers this spelling as a plain present of ziehen, to pull, and the entry is corrected for this tale. wer …, dem is the pattern “whoever …, to him”, each pronoun taking the case its own clause needs. verpflegen is to feed and care for someone.

sentences.t: Der dritte von den Burschen war aber der Kleinknecht, der ward von den andern für albern gehalten, dem gönnten sie die Mühle nicht; und er wollte sie hernach nicht einmal.
sentences.l: The third of the lads however was the under-servant, he was held by the others for silly, to that one they did not grant the mill; and he did not even want it afterward.
sentences.i: But the third of the lads was the under-servant, whom the others took for a simpleton, and they did not want him to have the mill; and afterwards he did not even want it.
sentences.n: der Kleinknecht is the lowest of the farm servants, the boy who does the small work. jemanden für albern halten is to take someone for a fool. jemandem etwas gönnen is to grant something willingly, and with nicht it is to grudge it. hernach is an older “afterwards”; the half-line gives away the end of the tale before it has begun.

sentences.t: Da zogen alle drei mit einander aus, und wie sie vor das Dorf kamen, sagten die zwei zu dem albernen Hans „du kannst nur hier bleiben, du kriegst dein Lebtag keinen Gaul.“
sentences.l: Then all three set out with one another, and when they came out before the village, the two said to the silly Hans “you can just stay here, you will not get a nag your life long.”
sentences.i: So all three set out together, and when they came out beyond the village the two said to silly Hans, “You may as well stay here — you will never get a horse as long as you live.”
sentences.n: ausziehen is separable: zogen … aus; the shared entry for zogen carries another tale’s sense and is corrected here. vor das Dorf kommen is to come out in front of the village, past the last houses. nur in a command is “just, only”, and it is not kindly meant. dein Lebtag is an old accusative of time, all your life. der Gaul is a plain workhorse, never a fine one.

sentences.t: Hans aber gieng doch mit, und als es Nacht war, kamen sie an eine Höhle, da hinein legten sie sich schlafen.
sentences.l: Hans however went along all the same, and when it was night, they came to a cave, in there they laid themselves to sleep.
sentences.i: But Hans went along all the same, and when night came they came to a cave, and lay down inside it to sleep.
sentences.n: mitgehen is separable: gieng … mit. doch is the particle of going against what has just been said. da hinein, “in there”, stands first and throws the verb ahead of its subject. sich schlafen legen is to lie down to sleep.

sentences.t: Die zwei Klugen warteten bis Hans eingeschlafen war,
sentences.l: The two clever ones waited until Hans had fallen asleep,
sentences.n: die Klugen is an adjective used as a noun, “the clever ones” — the tale names all three by their qualities more often than by their names. einschlafen forms its perfect with sein: war eingeschlafen.

sentences.t: dann stiegen sie auf, machten sich fort und ließen Hänschen liegen, und meintens recht fein gemacht zu haben;
sentences.l: then they got up, made themselves off and left little-Hans lying, and thought to have done it right finely;
sentences.i: then they got up, made off and left little Hans lying there, and thought they had managed it very neatly;
sentences.n: sich fortmachen is to make off. liegen lassen is to leave someone lying; the shared entry for ließen gives a quite different phrase and is corrected here. meintens is meinten es. recht fein is “right finely”, and Hänschen, the diminutive of Hans, is not affectionate in their mouths.

sentences.t: ja, es wird euch doch nicht gut gehen!
sentences.l: yes, it will not go well for you though!
sentences.i: ah, but it will not go well with you!
sentences.n: The narrator breaks in and speaks straight to the two, euch, “you”, although they cannot hear it. es geht jemandem gut is impersonal, with the person in the dative: things go well for someone. doch throws the sentence against what they have just congratulated themselves on.

sentences.t: Wie nun die Sonne kam, und Hans aufwachte, lag er in einer tiefen Höhle: er guckte sich überall um und rief „ach Gott, wo bin ich!“
sentences.l: When now the sun came, and Hans woke up, he lay in a deep cave: he looked himself around everywhere and cried “oh God, where am I!”
sentences.i: Now when the sun came and Hans woke, he was lying in a deep cave; he looked all about him and cried, “Oh God, where am I!”
sentences.n: sich umgucken is to look about one, separable: guckte … um. The exclamation mark stands where English would put a question mark — the 1857 text marks it as a cry rather than a question.

sentences.t: Da erhob er sich und krappelte die Höhle hinauf, gieng in den Wald und dachte „ich bin hier ganz allein und verlassen, wie soll ich nun zu einem Pferd kommen!“
sentences.l: Then he raised himself and scrabbled up out of the cave, went into the forest and thought “I am here quite alone and forsaken, how shall I now come by a horse!”
sentences.i: Then he got up and clambered up out of the cave, went into the forest and thought, “Here I am, quite alone and forsaken — how am I to come by a horse now?”
sentences.n: sich erheben is to raise oneself, to get up. krappeln is a country word for scrabbling or clambering, close to krabbeln, and one of the few dialect words in this tale; the shared glossary has it right. zu etwas kommen is to come by something, to get hold of it.

sentences.t: Indem er so in Gedanken dahin gieng, begegnete ihm ein kleines buntes Kätzchen, das sprach ganz freundlich „Hans, wo willst du hin!“
sentences.l: While he went along so in thoughts, there met him a little dappled kitten, that said quite kindly “Hans, where do you want to go!”
sentences.i: As he went along like that, deep in thought, a little dappled cat met him, and it said quite kindly, “Hans, where are you off to?”
sentences.n: indem here is the older “while”, not the modern “by doing”. begegnen takes the dative: ihm begegnete, “there met him”. wo willst du hin has no verb of motion at all — the hin carries it and wollen supplies the rest. bunt is dappled, of mixed colours.

sentences.t: „Ach, du kannst mir doch nicht helfen.“
sentences.l: “Oh, you cannot help me anyway.”
sentences.n: Hans answers without being named as the speaker, and without answering the question. helfen takes the dative, mir. doch is again the particle of resignation, “anyway, after all”.

sentences.t: „Was dein Begehren ist, weiß ich wohl,“ sprach das Kätzchen, „du willst einen hübschen Gaul haben.
sentences.l: “What your desire is, I know well,” said the kitten, “you want to have a handsome horse.
sentences.i: “I know well enough what you want,” said the kitten; “you want a good horse.
sentences.n: weiß here is the verb wissen, to know — the shared glossary answers this spelling with the adjective weiß, white, and the entry is corrected for this tale. das Begehren is the infinitive begehren, to desire, used as a noun. The object clause stands first, so ich comes after the verb.

sentences.t: Komm mit mir und sei sieben Jahre lang mein treuer Knecht, so will ich dir einen geben, schöner als du dein Lebtag einen gesehen hast.“
sentences.l: Come with me and be for seven years long my faithful servant, then I will give you one, finer than you have seen one your life long.”
sentences.i: Come with me and be my faithful servant for seven years, and I will give you one finer than any you have seen in all your life.”
sentences.n: sieben Jahre lang is an accusative of duration. so here is “then”, tying the command to its promise. einen is the pronoun “one”, standing for the horse, and German keeps it in the comparison where English drops it.

sentences.t: „Nun das ist eine wunderliche Katze,“ dachte Hans, „aber sehen will ich doch ob das wahr ist was sie sagt.“
sentences.l: “Well this is a strange cat,” thought Hans, “but see I will though whether it is true what she says.”
sentences.i: “Well, this is a strange cat,” thought Hans; “still, I mean to see whether what she says is true.”
sentences.n: sehen stands first for weight, which puts the subject behind the verb: sehen will ich. ob sends its verb to the end. die Katze is feminine, so German says sie, “she”, where English might say “it”.

sentences.t: Da nahm sie ihn mit in ihr verwünschtes Schlößchen und hatte da lauter Kätzchen, die ihr dienten: die sprangen flink die Treppe auf und ab, waren lustig und guter Dinge.
sentences.l: Then she took him along into her enchanted little castle and had there nothing but kittens that served her: those sprang nimbly up and down the stairs, were merry and of good spirits.
sentences.i: Then she took him along into her enchanted little castle, where she had nothing but kittens to serve her; they sprang nimbly up and down the stairs, and were merry and in good spirits.
sentences.n: mitnehmen is separable: nahm … mit. das Schlößchen is the diminutive of das Schloß, a castle; the shared glossary answers this spelling with the other Schloß, a lock or clasp, and the entry is corrected for this tale. lauter is “nothing but, sheer”. guter Dinge sein, “to be of good things”, is a frozen genitive for being in good spirits.

sentences.t: Abends, als sie sich zu Tisch setzten, mußten drei Musik machen:
sentences.l: In the evening, when they set themselves to table, three had to make music:
sentences.i: In the evening, when they sat down to table, three of them had to make music;
sentences.n: Abends is an adverbial genitive, “of an evening”. sich zu Tisch setzen, with no article, is the fixed phrase for sitting down to a meal. drei stands alone for “three of them”.

sentences.t: eins strich den Baß, das andere die Geige, das dritte setzte die Trompete an und blies die Backen auf so sehr es nur konnte.
sentences.l: one bowed the bass, the other the fiddle, the third set the trumpet to its lips and blew its cheeks out as much as ever it could.
sentences.i: one bowed the bass, another the fiddle, and the third set the trumpet to its lips and puffed out its cheeks as hard as ever it could.
sentences.n: streichen of a stringed instrument is to bow it, and the shared entry gives another sense of the verb, so it is corrected here. das andere has no verb of its own — strich carries all three players. ansetzen is to set an instrument to the lips, separable: setzte … an. Backen are cheeks; the shared glossary answers this spelling with backen, to bake, and that entry is corrected too. The kittens are eins, das andere, das dritte, all neuter, because Kätzchen is neuter.

sentences.t: Als sie gegessen hatten, wurde der Tisch weggetragen, und die Katze sagte „nun komm, Hans, und tanze mit mir.“
sentences.l: When they had eaten, the table was carried away, and the cat said “now come, Hans, and dance with me.”
sentences.n: wurde … weggetragen is a passive; the table is carried out bodily, as tables of boards and trestles were. tanze is an imperative to one person.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete er, „mit einer Miezekatze tanze ich nicht, das habe ich noch niemals gethan.“
sentences.l: “No,” he answered, “with a pussycat I do not dance, that I have never yet done.”
sentences.i: “No,” he answered, “I do not dance with a pussycat; I have never yet done such a thing.”
sentences.n: tanze here is the verb, first person singular — the shared glossary answers this spelling with the noun der Tanz in the dative, and the entry is corrected for this tale. Miezekatze is the nursery word for a cat, and in Hans’s mouth it makes the refusal ruder than it looks. gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan.

sentences.t: „So bringt ihn ins Bett“ sagte sie zu den Kätzchen.
sentences.l: “Then bring him to bed” she said to the kittens.
sentences.i: “Then put him to bed,” she said to the kittens.
sentences.n: so at the head of a command is “then, in that case”. bringt is the imperative to more than one. The 1857 text sets no comma before sagte.

sentences.t: Da leuchtete ihm eins in seine Schlafkammer, eins zog ihm die Schuhe aus, eins die Strümpfe und zuletzt blies eins das Licht aus.
sentences.l: Then one lighted him into his sleeping-chamber, one pulled his shoes off him, one the stockings and last one blew the light out.
sentences.i: Then one of them lighted him into his bedchamber, one pulled off his shoes, one his stockings, and last of all one blew out the light.
sentences.n: jemandem leuchten is to light the way for someone, the person standing in the dative. ausziehen is separable: zog … aus, and ihm is again the dative of the person the shoes belong to, where English says “his”. The third clause has no verb at all — zog does duty for it.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen kamen sie wieder und halfen ihm aus dem Bett:
sentences.l: On the other morning they came again and helped him out of the bed:
sentences.i: The next morning they came again and helped him out of bed;
sentences.n: am andern Morgen is “the next morning” — ander here is “the following”, not “different”. helfen takes the dative, ihm.

sentences.t: eins zog ihm die Strümpfe an, eins band ihm die Strumpfbänder, eins holte die Schuhe, eins wusch ihn und eins trocknete ihm mit dem Schwanz das Gesicht ab.
sentences.l: one pulled his stockings on him, one tied his garters for him, one fetched the shoes, one washed him and one dried his face off for him with its tail.
sentences.i: one pulled on his stockings, one tied his garters, one fetched his shoes, one washed him, and one dried his face with its tail.
sentences.n: band is the past of binden, to tie — the shared glossary answers this spelling with the noun das Band, a ribbon, and the entry is corrected for this tale. abtrocknen is separable, and its ab waits until the very end of the sentence. Each ihm is the dative of the person whose stockings, garters and face these are.

sentences.t: „Das thut recht sanft“ sagte Hans.
sentences.l: “That does right softly” said Hans.
sentences.i: “That feels good and gentle,” said Hans.
sentences.n: thut is the 1857 spelling of tut. thun with an adverb, said of a thing, describes how it feels or acts: das thut sanft. recht before an adverb is “good and, quite”.

sentences.t: Er mußte aber auch der Katze dienen und alle Tage Holz klein machen;
sentences.l: He had however also to serve the cat and every day to make wood small;
sentences.i: But he had to serve the cat too, and to chop wood small every day;
sentences.n: dienen takes the dative, der Katze. Holz klein machen is to split firewood — German says to make it small. alle Tage is an accusative of time, every day.

sentences.t: dazu kriegte er eine Axt von Silber, und die Keile und Säge von Silber, und der Schläger war von Kupfer.
sentences.l: for that he got an axe of silver, and the wedges and saw of silver, and the beetle was of copper.
sentences.i: for it he was given an axe of silver, and the wedges and the saw of silver, and the mallet was of copper.
sentences.n: von Silber, “of silver”, is how German names the stuff a thing is made of. die Keile are the wedges driven into a log to split it, and der Schläger is the heavy wooden beetle that drives them home. Silver makes a poor axe, which the tale does not trouble to say.

sentences.t: Nun, da machte ers klein, blieb da im Haus, hatte sein gutes Essen und Trinken, sah aber niemand als die bunte Katze und ihr Gesinde.
sentences.l: Well, so he made it small, stayed there in the house, had his good food and drink, but saw no one but the dappled cat and her household.
sentences.i: Well, so he chopped it small, stayed there in the house, and had his good food and drink, but saw no one except the dappled cat and her household.
sentences.n: ers is er es. Essen und Trinken are infinitives used as nouns, eating and drinking. das Gesinde is the whole body of servants of a house, an old collective word. niemand als is “no one but”.

sentences.t: Einmal sagte sie zu ihm „geh hin und mähe meine Wiese, und mache das Gras trocken,“
sentences.l: Once she said to him “go there and mow my meadow, and make the grass dry,”
sentences.n: hingehen is separable: geh … hin, “go off there”. mähe and mache are imperatives to one person. das Gras trocken machen is to make hay: the grass is cut and then dried.

sentences.t: und gab ihm von Silber eine Sense und von Gold einen Wetzstein, hieß ihn aber auch alles wieder richtig abliefern.
sentences.l: and gave him of silver a scythe and of gold a whetstone, but bade him also deliver everything back properly.
sentences.i: and gave him a scythe of silver and a whetstone of gold, but bade him hand it all back properly afterwards.
sentences.n: heißen with an accusative and an infinitive is to bid someone do something; the shared glossary answers hieß with “was called”, its commoner sense, and the entry is corrected for this tale. abliefern is to hand over or deliver up, said of tools and goods entrusted to one.

sentences.t: Da gieng Hans hin und that was ihm geheißen war; nach vollbrachter Arbeit trug er Sense, Wetzstein und Heu nach Haus, und fragte ob sie ihm noch nicht seinen Lohn geben wollte.
sentences.l: Then Hans went there and did what was bidden him; after accomplished work he carried scythe, whetstone and hay home, and asked whether she would not yet give him his wage.
sentences.i: So Hans went and did as he was bidden; the work done, he carried scythe, whetstone and hay home, and asked whether she would not give him his wage yet.
sentences.n: was ihm geheißen war is a passive of the same heißen: what he had been bidden. nach vollbrachter Arbeit is a compressed phrase, “the work being accomplished”. der Lohn is a servant’s wage, and here the wage is the horse.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sagte die Katze, „du sollst mir erst noch einerlei thun,
sentences.l: “No,” said the cat, “you shall first do one thing more for me,
sentences.i: “No,” said the cat, “you shall do one thing more for me first;
sentences.n: einerlei is here a noun, “one thing, one and the same”; modern German keeps the word only in the sense “all the same to me”. mir is a dative of interest, “for me”. thun is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: da ist Bauholz von Silber, Zimmeraxt, Winkeleisen und was nöthig ist, alles von Silber, daraus baue mir erst ein kleines Häuschen.“
sentences.l: there is building-timber of silver, carpenter’s-axe, angle-iron and what is necessary, all of silver, out of it build me first a little house.”
sentences.i: there is building timber of silver, a carpenter’s axe, a square and whatever is needed, all of silver — out of it build me a little house first.”
sentences.n: das Bauholz is timber for building. die Zimmeraxt is the carpenter’s broad axe, from Zimmer in its old sense of a piece of building work; das Winkeleisen is the iron square by which right angles are set out. nöthig is the 1857 spelling of nötig. baue is an imperative to one person, and daraus, “out of it”, stands first.

sentences.t: Da baute Hans das Häuschen fertig und sagte er hätte nun alles gethan, und hätte noch kein Pferd.
sentences.l: Then Hans built the little house finished and said he had now done everything, and had still no horse.
sentences.i: So Hans built the little house and finished it, and said that he had now done everything and still had no horse.
sentences.n: fertig bauen is to build a thing to completion, the adjective joining the verb where English adds a clause. hätte twice over is the subjunctive of reported speech, marking the words as his and not the narrator’s.

sentences.t: Doch waren ihm die sieben Jahre herumgegangen wie ein halbes.
sentences.l: Yet the seven years had gone round for him like a half [year].
sentences.i: Yet the seven years had gone by for him like half a year.
sentences.n: ihm is the dative of the person the time passed for. herumgehen, of time, is to go round, to pass. ein halbes stands alone with Jahr unsaid, so the literal supplies [year] in square brackets.

sentences.t: Fragte die Katze ob er ihre Pferde sehen wollte?
sentences.l: Asked the cat whether he wanted to see her horses?
sentences.i: The cat asked whether he would like to see her horses.
sentences.n: The sentence begins with its verb and no pronoun at all, a quick narrative turn this tale is fond of. The question mark stands although the sentence only reports a question — the 1857 printing does this more than once.

sentences.t: „Ja“ sagte Hans.
sentences.l: “Yes” said Hans.
sentences.n: No comma before sagte and none after Ja: the 1857 text punctuates speech very lightly.

sentences.t: Da machte sie ihm das Häuschen auf, und weil sie die Thüre so aufmacht, da stehen zwölf Pferde,
sentences.l: Then she opened the little house for him, and as she opens the door so, there stand twelve horses,
sentences.i: Then she opened the little house for him, and the moment she opens the door, there stand twelve horses,
sentences.n: aufmachen is separable: machte … auf. In the middle of the sentence the tale slips into the present, aufmacht and stehen, the way a teller does when the story quickens, and the literal keeps the shift. Thüre is the 1857 spelling of Türe.

sentences.t: ach, die waren gewesen ganz stolz, die hatten geblänkt und gespiegelt, daß sich sein Herz im Leibe darüber freute.
sentences.l: ah, those had been quite proud, those had shone and glistened, so that his heart in his body rejoiced over it.
sentences.i: ah, they were splendid creatures, and they shone and glistened so that his heart rejoiced within him.
sentences.n: waren gewesen is a pluperfect where the sense wants a plain past — the loose speech of a teller rather than a fault in the text. blänken is an older form of blinken, to shine; spiegeln is to give the light back like a mirror. sich freuen is reflexive, and im Leibe, “in the body”, is where German puts a heart that is glad.

sentences.t: Nun gab sie ihm zu essen und zu trinken und sprach „geh heim, dein Pferd geb ich dir nicht mit: in drei Tagen aber komm ich und bringe dirs nach.“
sentences.l: Now she gave him to eat and to drink and said “go home, your horse I do not give you along: in three days however I come and bring it after you.”
sentences.i: Then she gave him food and drink and said, “Go home; I will not send your horse with you, but in three days I will come and bring it after you.”
sentences.n: zu essen geben, to give someone to eat, is the plain German for feeding a person. mitgeben is to give something along with someone, nachbringen to bring it after; both are separable. dirs is dir es. The present tense komm and bringe does duty for the future.

sentences.t: Also machte Hans sich auf, und sie zeigte ihm den Weg zur Mühle.
sentences.l: So Hans set himself out, and she showed him the way to the mill.
sentences.i: So Hans set out, and she showed him the way to the mill.
sentences.n: sich aufmachen is to set out, separable: machte … auf. also is the old “so, thus”, never English “also”.

sentences.t: Sie hatte ihm aber nicht einmal ein neues Kleid gegeben, sondern er mußte sein altes lumpiges Kittelchen behalten, das er mitgebracht hatte, und das ihm in den sieben Jahren überall zu kurz geworden war.
sentences.l: She had however not even given him a new garment, but rather he had to keep his old raggedy little smock that he had brought along, and that had become too short for him everywhere in the seven years.
sentences.i: But she had not even given him a new coat; he had to keep the old ragged little smock he had brought with him, which in the seven years had grown too short for him everywhere.
sentences.n: das Kleid is any garment, not only a dress. lumpig, from der Lumpen, a rag, is raggedy. das Kittelchen is the diminutive of der Kittel, a workman’s smock, and here the diminutive pities rather than fondles. überall zu kurz geworden, grown too short everywhere, is the plainest way of saying that he has grown.

sentences.t: Wie er nun heim kam, so waren die beiden andern Müllerburschen auch wieder da: jeder hatte zwar sein Pferd mitgebracht, aber des einen seins war blind, des andern seins lahm.
sentences.l: When he now came home, so the two other miller’s-lads were also there again: each had indeed brought his horse along, but the one’s was blind, the other’s lame.
sentences.i: Now when he came home, the two other miller’s lads were back as well; each had indeed brought a horse, but the one’s was blind and the other’s lame.
sentences.n: so at the head of the main clause, after a wie-clause, is a resumptive “then” that English simply leaves out. zwar … aber is “indeed … but”. des einen seins is an old homely possessive, “the one his one”, where modern German says das des einen.

sentences.t: Sie fragten „Hans, wo hast du dein Pferd?“
sentences.l: They asked “Hans, where have you your horse?”
sentences.i: They asked, “Hans, where is your horse?”
sentences.n: wo hast du … is “where have you”, where English prefers “where is”; German needs no auxiliary for the question.

sentences.t: „In drei Tagen wirds nachkommen.“
sentences.l: “In three days it will come after.”
sentences.i: “In three days it will come along after me.”
sentences.n: wirds is wird es. nachkommen is to come after, to follow on; it is separable, though after werden the infinitive keeps its particle.

sentences.t: Da lachten sie und sagten „ja du Hans, wo willst du ein Pferd herkriegen, das wird was rechtes sein!“
sentences.l: Then they laughed and said “yes you Hans, where do you want to get a horse from, that will be something fine!”
sentences.i: Then they laughed and said, “Oh yes, Hans — where are you to get a horse from? That will be a fine one!”
sentences.n: du Hans, with the pronoun before the name, is a mocking form of address. herkriegen is to get hold of from somewhere, the her- pointing back toward the speaker. was rechtes, “something fine”, is meant flat opposite, and the exclamation mark carries the sneer.

sentences.t: Hans gieng in die Stube, der Müller sagte aber er sollte nicht an den Tisch kommen, er wäre so zerrissen und zerlumpt, man müßte sich schämen, wenn jemand herein käme.
sentences.l: Hans went into the parlour, but the miller said he should not come to the table, he was so torn and tattered, one would have to be ashamed if anyone came in.
sentences.i: Hans went into the parlour, but the miller said he was not to come to the table — he was so torn and tattered that they would have to be ashamed if anyone came in.
sentences.n: wäre, müßte and käme are all subjunctives of reported speech: these are the miller’s words, not the tale’s judgement. zerrissen is a participle used as an adjective, torn, in tatters; the shared entry treats it as a past tense and is corrected here. sich schämen is to be ashamed.

sentences.t: Da gaben sie ihm ein bischen Essen hinaus, und wie sie Abends schlafen giengen, wollten ihm die zwei andern kein Bett geben,
sentences.l: Then they gave him a bit of food out, and when they went to sleep in the evening, the two others would not give him a bed,
sentences.i: So they handed him a bit of food outside, and when they went to bed in the evening the two others would not give him a bed,
sentences.n: hinausgeben is to hand something out to someone who is outside the room, and the little word hinaus says where Hans is eating. bischen is the 1857 spelling of bisschen. schlafen gehen is to go to bed.

sentences.t: und er mußte endlich ins Gänseställchen kriechen und sich auf ein wenig hartes Stroh legen.
sentences.l: and he had at last to creep into the little goose-stall and lay himself on a little hard straw.
sentences.i: and at last he had to creep into the little goose-house and lie down on a little hard straw.
sentences.n: das Gänseställchen is the diminutive of der Gänsestall, the goose-house, and the diminutive makes it meaner still. ein wenig is “a little”, with hartes Stroh standing after it under no article. sich legen is to lie down.

sentences.t: Am Morgen, wie er aufwacht, sind schon die drei Tage herum,
sentences.l: In the morning, as he wakes up, the three days are already round,
sentences.i: In the morning, as he wakes, the three days are already up,
sentences.n: The tale turns to the present tense here and stays in it, on and off, to the end — the teller draws close to the scene. herum sein, of a span of time, is to be up, over.

sentences.t: und es kommt eine Kutsche mit sechs Pferden, ei, die glänzten, daß es schön war, und ein Bedienter, der brachte noch ein siebentes, das war für den armen Müllerbursch.
sentences.l: and there comes a coach with six horses, ah, they gleamed so that it was a fine thing, and a servant, he brought yet a seventh, that was for the poor miller’s-lad.
sentences.i: and a coach comes with six horses — ah, how they gleamed, it was a fine sight — and a servant, and he brought a seventh besides, and that one was for the poor miller’s lad.
sentences.n: es kommt is the empty es that lets the real subject follow: “there comes”. daß es schön war, “so that it was fine”, is the tale’s plainest praise. der and das are demonstratives where English would use relatives. The tense slides back into the past in mid-sentence, and the telling is none the worse for it.

sentences.t: Aus der Kutsche aber stieg eine prächtige Königstochter und gieng in die Mühle hinein, und die Königstochter war das kleine bunte Kätzchen, dem der arme Hans sieben Jahr gedient hatte.
sentences.l: But out of the coach stepped a magnificent king’s-daughter and went into the mill, and the king’s-daughter was the little dappled kitten, whom poor Hans had served seven years.
sentences.i: But out of the coach stepped a splendid king’s daughter and went into the mill, and the king’s daughter was the little dappled cat that poor Hans had served for seven years.
sentences.n: Königstochter, king’s daughter, is the tale’s word for a princess and says plainly whose daughter she is. dem is a dative relative pronoun because dienen takes the dative, and it is neuter to agree with Kätzchen — grammatically the cat is still an it. sieben Jahr, with no plural ending, is an old measure phrase.

sentences.t: Sie fragte den Müller wo der Mahlbursch, der Kleinknecht wäre?
sentences.l: She asked the miller where the grinding-lad, the under-servant, was?
sentences.i: She asked the miller where the grinding lad was, the under-servant.
sentences.n: der Mahlbursch, from mahlen, to grind, is the lad who works at the millstones; the tale uses it beside Müllerbursch with no difference of meaning. wäre is the subjunctive of her question, and again the question mark stands over a sentence that only reports one.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Müller „den können wir nicht in die Mühle nehmen, der ist so verrissen und liegt im Gänsestall.“
sentences.l: Then the miller said “that one we cannot take into the mill, that one is so torn and lies in the goose-stall.”
sentences.i: Then the miller said, “That one we cannot have in the mill; he is so ragged, and he lies in the goose-house.”
sentences.n: den and der at the head of their clauses are demonstratives, “that one”, and used of a person they are dismissive. verrissen, torn to pieces, is stronger than the zerrissen of a moment ago, and it is said of the man rather than of his clothes.

sentences.t: Da sagte die Königstochter sie sollten ihn gleich holen.
sentences.l: Then the king’s-daughter said they should fetch him at once.
sentences.n: sollten is the subjunctive of her order in reported speech. gleich is “at once, straight away”. She gives the order to the household without a word of explanation, and the tale gives none either.

sentences.t: Also holten sie ihn heraus, und er mußte sein Kittelchen zusammenpacken, um sich zu bedecken.
sentences.l: So they fetched him out, and he had to gather his little smock together, in order to cover himself.
sentences.i: So they fetched him out, and he had to gather his little smock about him to cover himself.
sentences.n: zusammenpacken is to bundle together — the smock is so short now that he must hold it together. um … zu is “in order to”, with the zu-infinitive at the end.

sentences.t: Da schnallte der Bediente prächtige Kleider aus, und mußte ihn waschen und anziehen, und wie er fertig war, konnte kein König schöner aussehen.
sentences.l: Then the servant unbuckled magnificent clothes, and had to wash him and dress him, and when he was ready, no king could look finer.
sentences.i: Then the servant unstrapped splendid clothes, and had to wash him and dress him, and when he was ready, no king could have looked finer.
sentences.n: ausschnallen is to undo the straps of a bundle or trunk and take out what is inside; the shared entry for schnallte gives the opposite, buckling something on, and is corrected here. mußte takes no new subject — it is still the servant. kein König schöner is “no king finer”, the comparative standing without than.

sentences.t: Danach verlangte die Jungfrau die Pferde zu sehen, welche die andern Mahlburschen mitgebracht hatten, eins war blind, das andere lahm.
sentences.l: After that the maiden demanded to see the horses which the other grinding-lads had brought along, one was blind, the other lame.
sentences.i: After that the maiden asked to see the horses the other grinding lads had brought, and one was blind, the other lame.
sentences.n: die Jungfrau, the maiden, is the third word the tale has found for her in as many sentences. welche is the older relative pronoun where modern German prefers die. The last clause simply stands beside the rest with no “and” to join it.

sentences.t: Da ließ sie den Bedienten das siebente Pferd bringen: wie der Müller das sah, sprach er so eins wär ihm noch nicht auf den Hof gekommen; „und das ist für den dritten Mahlbursch“ sagte sie.
sentences.l: Then she had the servant bring the seventh horse: when the miller saw that, he said such a one had not yet come onto his yard; “and that is for the third grinding-lad” said she.
sentences.i: Then she had the servant bring the seventh horse; and when the miller saw it he said that such a one had never yet come into his yard. “And that is for the third grinding lad,” she said.
sentences.n: lassen with an infinitive is to have something done. so eins is “such a one”. wär is wäre, the subjunctive of reported speech, and ihm auf den Hof kommen puts the owner of the yard in the dative.

sentences.t: „Da muß er die Mühle haben,“ sagte der Müller,
sentences.l: “Then he must have the mill,” said the miller,
sentences.n: da here is “in that case, then”, not “there”. The miller keeps to his own bargain the moment the horse is standing in front of him.

sentences.t: die Königstochter aber sprach da wäre das Pferd, er sollte seine Mühle auch behalten: und nimmt ihren treuen Hans und setzt ihn in die Kutsche und fährt mit ihm fort.
sentences.l: but the king’s-daughter said there was the horse, he should keep his mill as well: and takes her faithful Hans and sets him in the coach and drives away with him.
sentences.i: but the king’s daughter said that there was the horse, and that he might keep his mill too; and she takes her faithful Hans and sets him in the coach and drives away with him.
sentences.n: wäre and sollte are subjunctives of reported speech. After the colon the tale goes over into the present and stays there — nimmt, setzt, fährt — and the three ands run the ending together in one breath. setzt is a third person present, “sets”; the shared entry calls it an imperative and is corrected for this tale. fortfahren is separable, and its fort closes the sentence.

sentences.t: Sie fahren zuerst nach dem kleinen Häuschen, das er mit dem silbernen Werkzeug gebaut hat, da ist es ein großes Schloß, und ist alles darin von Silber und Gold;
sentences.l: They drive first to the little house that he has built with the silver tools, there it is a great castle, and is everything in it of silver and gold;
sentences.i: They drive first to the little house he had built with the silver tools, and there it is a great castle, and everything in it is of silver and gold;
sentences.n: das Werkzeug is a singular noun for a whole set of tools. da ist es ein großes Schloß — the little house has become a castle in the meantime, and the tale reports it as flatly as it would report the weather. The last clause drops its subject es, and the literal keeps the gap.

sentences.t: und da hat sie ihn geheirathet, und war er reich, so reich, daß er für sein Lebtag genug hatte.
sentences.l: and there she has married him, and he was rich, so rich that he had enough for his life long.
sentences.i: and there she married him, and he was rich, so rich that he had enough for all his life.
sentences.n: geheirathet is the 1857 spelling of geheiratet. The tense shifts inside the sentence, from perfect to plain past. reich is the adjective rich; the shared glossary answers this spelling with the noun das Reich, a realm, and the entry is corrected for this tale. für sein Lebtag is the very phrase the two lads mocked him with at the start.

sentences.t: Darum soll keiner sagen daß wer albern ist deshalb nichts rechtes werden könne.
sentences.l: Therefore no one shall say that whoever is silly can for that reason become nothing fine.
sentences.i: So let no one say that a man who is a simpleton can come to nothing on that account.
sentences.n: The tale ends on a moral, and gives it one sentence and no more. wer albern ist, “whoever is silly”, is a clause standing as the subject inside the daß-clause. könne is the subjunctive of reported speech, marking this as the sort of thing people say. nichts rechtes werden is to come to nothing, to make nothing of oneself.

glossary.alter: alt — old (masc. nom. adj.; ein alter Müller)
glossary.backen: die Backe — cheeks (acc. pl.; die Backen aufblasen: to puff out one’s cheeks)
glossary.band: binden — tied, bound (3rd sg. past); also das Band — ribbon, band
glossary.bringt: bringen — bring! (imperative pl.: bringt ihn ins Bett); also: brings (3rd sg. present)
glossary.dahin: dahin — along, onward (dahin gehen: to walk along); also: to that point
glossary.einerlei: einerlei — one thing, one and the same (here a noun); otherwise: all the same, all one
glossary.eins: eins — one, one of them (neuter, of the Kätzchen: eins … das andere … das dritte; so eins: such a one)
glossary.hieß: heißen — bade, told (3rd sg. past, with an accusative and an infinitive); also: was called
glossary.ließen: lassen — left (3rd pl. past; liegen lassen: to leave lying)
glossary.pferde: das Pferd — horses (nom./acc. pl.; zwölf Pferde)
glossary.reich: reich — rich (adjective); also das Reich — realm, kingdom
glossary.schlößchen: das Schlößchen — little castle (diminutive of das Schloß, castle; 1857 spelling of Schlösschen)
glossary.schnallte: ausschnallen — unbuckled, unstrapped (3rd sg. past; separable aus-: schnallte … aus)
glossary.schöner: schön — finer, more beautiful (comparative; schöner als: finer than); also schöner: fine (masc. adj.)
glossary.setzt: setzen — sets, places (3rd sg. present; setzt ihn in die Kutsche)
glossary.setzte: ansetzen — set (an instrument) to the lips (3rd sg. past; separable an-: setzte … an)
glossary.strich: streichen — bowed, drew the bow across (3rd sg. past; den Baß streichen: to bow the bass)
glossary.tanze: tanzen — dance (1st sg. present, and the imperative sg.: tanze mit mir); also der Tanz — dance
glossary.weiß: wissen — know (1st sg. present); also weiß: white
glossary.zerrissen: zerrissen — torn, in tatters (past participle of zerreißen used as an adjective)
glossary.zieht: ausziehen — set out! (imperative pl.; separable aus-: zieht aus)
glossary.zog: ziehen — pulled (3rd sg. past); zog … aus: pulled off, zog … an: pulled on (of clothes)
glossary.zogen: ausziehen — set out (3rd pl. past; separable aus-: zogen … aus)
